prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock based on magic-wavelength trapping and its development to a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18

statement.case_for: I keep B022 with Katori and Ye as a single prize part, and after the full first-round exchange I hold it with more confidence than before, because the eight written cases give the same physical picture from different fields. The magic-wavelength condition cancels the differential light shift while the lattice removes Doppler and recoil broadening, so thousands of neutral atoms are interrogated at once. That gives stability that a single ion cannot reach. Ye's group, and then groups at RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE and NIST, controlled the systematics to about 10^-18, and clock-to-clock comparisons agree. For me this independent reproduction is the decisive maturity test, the same one I apply when different DFT codes must agree on a solid. The remaining systematics (blackbody shift, polarizabilities, collisional shifts) are computable from atomic structure theory and checked against measurement, so the result is understood and not merely working. Delivered physics already exists: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, a Fermi-degenerate many-body clock regime, and strict limits on varying constants and ultralight dark matter. The credit is the cleanest on the shortlist, with one name for the concept and first demonstrations and one for the record regime.
statement.case_against: The honest weakness is the one the chair's summary records: this is a measurement advance, and the largest returns (dark matter, constants, geodesy) are still limits and consistency checks, with no new effect observed. I would be more comfortable if the citation made explicit what was learned, so I propose naming the principle (magic-wavelength trapping) and the performance. The lineage worry about the 2005 comb prize and 2012 ion-control prize also has not gone away for me. I think it is answered by the different physical route, many neutral atoms at once, but a sceptical reader may still see an increment. The redefinition of the second has not happened, and uncredited contributors (Lemonde, Gill, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom) cannot be settled from the packet. I accept a two-name award as an imperfect but defensible cut, since the committee has to attach a prize to the decisive steps and not to the whole field.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, asks whether the credit can be written down, and says the Metzner omission in B018 is a structural difficulty because the committee would recognise a framework while excluding one of its originators. He also records that the discovery content of B022 so far is mostly upper limits and consistency tests.
responses.response: I accept your point on B018 and I no longer carry it as a preferred configuration. DMFT is a controlled framework in my field, but Metzner's missing name means the citation cannot be written honestly, and adding a fourth name breaks the three-person limit. On your second point I agree that B022 has delivered limits and not a new effect. I answer it by the content of the citation. The demonstrated results are an unambiguous fact: the 10^-18 level reproduced across laboratories, the millimetre gravitational redshift and the many-body clock regime. A prize for a verified quantitative capability that rests on well understood atomic physics is defensible even without a new phenomenon, and I would rather say that plainly than overclaim discovery.

responses.point: Kroll prefers the wording 'invention and realisation' of the lattice clock, stresses that a many-atom clock gives statistics a single ion cannot, and discloses a mild personal link to the B022 community through a year in John Hall's laboratory and Hall's long collaboration with Jun Ye.
responses.response: I agree with your physical argument that many atoms at the magic wavelength give a statistical advantage unavailable to a single ion, and I think it is the cleanest way to separate this prize from 2012. On the disclosure, I regard it as a mild, indirect link, since you state no collaboration or supervisory tie to Katori or Ye, and I see no need for a step beyond disclosure; I would not ask for a recusal. On the wording, I prefer naming magic-wavelength trapping in the citation, as Olsson does, over the bare phrase 'realisation', because the cancellation of the light shift is the scientific content that distinguishes the clock from its predecessors. I could live with your wording if the committee prefers it.

responses.point: Danielsson reads the lattice clock as a clue pulled from nature by measurement, wants the citation to say it opens new precision tests, and keeps B028 and B020 as alternatives.
responses.response: I share your reading of the content, but I would not put a forward-looking phrase such as 'opening new precision tests' into the citation, because the committee cannot know what those tests will find, and Pearce's point about upper limits applies. I would write what has been demonstrated, namely the invention and the 10^-18 performance. We agree on the fallbacks. B028 is the condensed-matter surprise I value, but I remain unsure it is ready, since the superconducting mechanism is not understood and the experimental first authors are not credited. B020 is the stronger second choice if the committee set shrinks to Bloch, Greiner and Zoller, though I defer to the atomic physicists on whether those three names are complete.

responses.point: Mehlig rejects DMFT as an approximation scheme exact only in infinite dimensions, and says B011 is physically distinct from the 2016 vortex-unbinding prize but should not displace a candidate with broad support.
responses.response: We now agree on the substance, even though I defended B018 in round 1. Its accuracy for low-dimensional and non-local correlations is limited, and that is a fair reading of what a method is worth. I still think your B011 deserves recognition at some point, so I will not dismiss it, but I read the 2016 overlap and the uneven experimental confirmation as reasons it is less mature than B022 this year. Your own move toward B022, on the grounds that the mechanism is identified and understood and not only popular, matches how I reached the same position, and I do not treat the support count as the argument.

responses.point: Lindroth, from atomic physics, finds the clock physics fully interpretable, notes that the weighting between Katori's concept and the JILA record performance has to be settled, and explicitly resists widening the credit beyond two names.
responses.response: I rely on your judgement here since atomic metrology is outside my field. I agree with you on credit: the cleanest weighting is to give Katori the concept and first demonstrations and Ye the path to the record regime, and the citation should include both elements so neither is a footnote. Widening beyond two names would require primary evidence for Lemonde or Gill that none of us has in the packet, and I would not trade a clean award for an uncertain one. If a colleague wants to substitute a name, the evidence should be about the magic-wavelength proposal and first lattice demonstration, and that evidence should be put in front of us before the vote.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts a verified measurement capability as sufficient scientific weight when the delivered physics is mostly limits and consistency tests, and whether it prefers to wait for the SI redefinition of the second.

Whether Katori's priority and the Ye/JILA record performance are weighted correctly, and whether Lemonde, Gill or another early lattice-clock contributor has stronger primary-source claims than the packet shows.
How strongly the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes weigh against the lattice clock in the final vote, even if the physical route is different.
If the committee adds a second part, whether B020 can be reduced to a defensible set of three names, and whether B028 is early because the pairing mechanism is unsettled.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict or recusal to disclose. My field is first-principles electronic-structure theory and magnetism, and I have no collaboration, institutional or supervisory link to Katori, Ye or any other credited person on the shortlist. I have read Kroll's disclosure of his link through John Hall and consider disclosure sufficient. I stay far from the atomic-metrology details and defer to Lindroth, Kroll and Danielsson on priority.
